_comment: Hand-verified input/output pairs. Each is computed independently of the spec's `compute` and then asserted by scripts/verify-formula-specs.mjs. This is the only check that can catch a formula that is internally self-consistent but physically wrong - the 200-sample sweep proves the math does not crash and does not collapse, but it happily accepts a land-soaking requirement of 32,000 mm. Add a case for every spec; use `tolerance` for rounded results.

a-pto-power._note: BP x eta_trans. 50 kW x 0.90 = 45 kW

a-specific-fuel-consumption._note: mf/(P x t). 12 kg / (40 kW x 3 h) = 0.1 kg/kWh

b-irrigation-interval._note: Dad/Cu. 60 mm / 5 mm per day = 12 days

b-lsr-net._note: rb x d x theta_r + h_sw. 1.3 g/cm3 x 200 mm x 0.20 = 52 mm, + 30 mm ponded = 82 mm. A physically sane land-soaking requirement is tens of mm, not thousands.

c-sensible-heat._note: m Cp dT. 100 kg x 4.18 kJ/kgC x 50 C = 20900 kJ

c-ohms-law._note: I x R. 5 A x 220 ohm = 1100 V

c-electrical-energy._note: P x t. 2.5 kW x 8 h = 20 kWh

c-power-factor._note: P/S. 90/100 = 0.9. A power factor is dimensionless and never exceeds 1, so real power must stay below apparent power.

a-belt-center-distance._note: solve 2C + (pi/2)(550) + 62500/(4C) = 2000 for C; forward check must return 2000

a-chain-length._note: solve L = 2C + a + b/C = 300 for C; forward check must return 300

a-mass-flow-rate._note: Q_m = v A rho = 1.5 x 0.05 x 1000 kg/s

a-windpump-solar-insolation._note: I = P_o x T = 3.5 x 5.5 kWh/day

b-water-applied-depth._note: volume route: 1.5 ha x 10000 m2/ha x 0.08 m = 1200 m3 over 6 h = 200 m3/h = 200000 L/3600 s = 55.5556 L/s. The printed-rounded coefficient 27.78 gives exactly 55.56, the same to 2 decimals; the exact coefficient is 1000/36 = 27.7778

b-runoff-volume._note: 850 L/s x 1.5 h x 3600 s/h / 1000 L per m3 = 4590 m3; the printed 0.278 would give 354.6, which is 1/3.6 of the answer

b-soil-total-volume._note: 200 + 500 + 1500 = 2200 cm3. Cross-check from the other side: the void part is 200 + 500 = 700 and the solid part 1500, and 700 + 1500 = 2200, so the three-phase total agrees with void + solid.

b-soil-volume-of-voids._note: 300 + 450 = 750 cm3. The 1500 cm3 core of the porosity case then holds 750 of voids and 750 of solids, so e = 750/750 = 1.0 - the boundary of a very loose sand, consistent with a high 0.5 porosity rather than a contradiction.

b-soil-weight._note: 0.3 + 450 + 1000 = 1450.3 g. The 0.3 g of air is 0.02% of the total, so dropping it shifts the answer by less than a gram and cannot be seen in any rendered option. That is why it is recorded in `mistakes` instead of being offered as a distractor, where it would collide with the correct value after rounding.

b-porosity._note: 450/1500 = 0.3. Cross-check with the density form 1 - D_b/D_p: for 0.3 it needs D_b/D_p = 0.7, so D_b = 0.7 x 2.65 = 1.855 g/cm3, which is loose for a cultivated soil and consistent with the 0.3 porosity the handbook quotes for a sandy loam.

b-moisture-content-wet-basis._note: 75/300 = 0.25, so 0.25 x 100 = 25.0%. The dry basis on the same sample is 75/(300 - 75) x 100 = 33.3%, which is the 1/(1 - 0.25) = 1.333x relationship. The two bases differ by a third here, so the dry-basis distractor stays clearly distinct after rounding.

b-particle-density._note: 300/120 = 2.5 g/cm3. Textbook quartz is 2.65; 2.5 is on the low side and is what a soil carrying clay or organic matter gives, since both pull the average down. Dividing by the bulk volume instead would have returned 1.4, the apparent specific gravity of the other case.

b-void-ratio._note: 480/1200 = 0.4. Consistency check by converting to porosity: n = e/(1 + e) = 0.4/1.4 = 0.2857, and the same sample read as a porosity gives 480/(480 + 1200) = 0.2857. The two agree to four decimals, so e is not a mislabelled n.

b-apparent-specific-gravity._note: 1.40/1.00 = 1.4. Paired with the real specific gravity of 2.65 the porosity is 1 - 1.4/2.65 = 0.4717, a normal sandy loam, which is the physical sanity check on both densities at once.

b-real-specific-gravity._note: 2.65/1.00 = 2.65, the textbook value for quartz. The divisor is the sampled water density and not a written 1.0, so a D_w of 0.99 would give 2.6768 - the 1% shift the water-density range exists to exercise, and the reason the two specific gravities are separate formulas.

b-lsr-gross._note: 50 + 5 + 12 = 67 mm. Both losses are added, so the gross figure sits above the net one; the 17 mm of ET plus percolation is 34% of what the farmer asked for and 25% of what the pump must deliver, which is the gap a canal operator has to cover.

b-water-power._note: 9810 * 0.5 * 20 * 0.85 = 83,385 W = 83.385 kW. Step by step: 9810 * 0.5 = 4905 N/s per metre of head, times 20 m = 98,100 W of hydraulic power, times 0.85 for turbine efficiency = 83,385 W. Dropping k would give 98,100 W, which is the 1/k = 1.176x distractor.

b-total-dynamic-head._note: 12.0 + 0.45 + 3.2 + 8.0 = 23.65 m. Cross-check: the static lift is 12.0 of that, so the working losses (velocity + friction + pressure) add 11.65 m, slightly under half the total. A pump sized on the 12 m lift alone would be short by 11.65 m on this line.

b-static-head._note: 25 - 6 = 19 m. The source water surface is 25 m above the pump and the junction of lateral and main is 6 m above the same pump, so the water surface stands 19 m above the junction. Adding instead of subtracting would give 31 m, which is the 31/19 = 1.63x distractor.

b-pressure-head._note: 196200/9810 = 20.0 m exactly. Physical check: 196.2 kPa is 2 atm, and the textbook height of a water column under 2 atm of pressure is 20 m, so the specific weight 9810 N/m3 and the answer agree with the standard atmosphere rather than only with themselves. Dividing by 1000 instead would give 196.2 m, the 9.81x distractor.

b-friction-head._note: 2.5 + 0.35 = 2.85 m. The main carries the whole flow and so accounts for 2.5 of the 2.85 m, about 88%; the lateral is the remaining 0.35 m. That ratio is why keeping only the lateral cannot be offered as an option - it is 12% here and falls to 0.4% at the far end of the sampled ranges.

b-net-application-depth._note: Available water FC - PWP = 0.32 - 0.14 = 0.18 of the pore space. Then 0.18 * 1.45 = 0.261 kg of water per m3 of bulk soil, * 0.60 m root zone = 0.1566 m, * 0.50 MAD = 0.0783 m. So 78.3 mm is applied, which is 43% of the full 0.1566 m the profile could hold - the management allowable depletion is the safety margin, so the applied depth is always less than the available water.

b-gross-application-depth._note: 60/0.75 = 80 mm. The 20 mm difference between net and gross is the quarter of the applied water that never reaches the root zone. Entering EA as 75 instead of 0.75 would give 0.8 mm, which is the percentage mistake the spec teaches in mistakes.

b-time-of-application._note: 2000 m2 * 0.05 m = 100 m3 of water needed; 100 / 0.025 m3/s = 4000 s, which is 66.7 minutes or 1.11 hours. Units check: m2 * m = m3, and m3 / (m3/s) = s, so the answer is already in seconds with no hidden factor. The whole set moves at 25 L/s, a realistic trickle-drip flow for 0.05 ha.

b-application-efficiency._note: 120 - (12 + 6 + 4) = 98, and 98/120 = 0.81667. The three losses total 22 L/s, 18.3% of what entered, so efficiency is the complement. Seepage alone is 12 of the 22, over half the loss, which is the term that moves with soil texture. Tolerance is stated because 98/120 is a repeating decimal.

b-border-irrigation-stream._note: 0.0025 * 2^(-0.75) = 0.0025 * 0.5946035575 = 0.0014865089 ft3/s per unit width. 2^0.75 = 1.6817928, so the reciprocal is 0.5946036. Check the sign of the exponent against the handbook: a steeper border must take a SMALLER stream, and doubling the slope here drops the stream to 0.59 of its value, so a positive exponent would be backwards. The 0.011 constant would give 0.0065378, the 4.4x distractor. Tolerance stated because the exponent is irrational.

b-farm-irrigation-requirement._note: CWR + LR - ERF = 420 + 45 - 130 = 335 mm. Rain is SUBTRACTED, so a bigger effective rainfall lowers the requirement; adding it instead would give 595, which is the first distractor. The leaching term still adds on top.
640 + 25 - 85 = 580 mm. Same two-sign check as the first case: 85 of rain comes off, 25 of leaching goes on.

b-farm-water-requirement._note: FIR + Losses = 320 + 140 = 460 mm. The total must exceed the requirement it serves by exactly the loss, so the bare 320 is one of the distractors and is 0.70x.
180 + 95 = 275 mm. Here the loss is 0.35 of the total, the low end of the 80..250 mm loss range against a 150..600 mm requirement.

b-diversion-water-requirement._note: FWR + CL = 480 + 210 = 690 mm. Conveyance loss is added as a depth, not applied as a percentage of the farm requirement.
250 + 120 = 370 mm. The loss is nearly half the farm requirement, which is the point of the formula for a long unlined earth canal.

b-farm-turnout-requirement._note: FWR + FDL = 560 + 115 = 675 mm. Third step in the chain (CWR -> FWR -> DWR -> FTR); each step adds the loss incurred past the previous point.
300 + 70 = 370 mm. 70 mm of ditch loss on a 300 mm requirement is a 0.23 ratio, near the low end.

b-depth-readily-available-moisture._note: Same printed product as b-net-application-depth. 0.32 - 0.14 = 0.18 plant-available fraction; x1.45 apparent specific gravity = 0.261; x0.60 m root zone = 0.1566 m; x0.45 allowable depletion = 0.070470 m, which rounds to 0.0705. Tolerance stated for the 4-dp rounding.
0.30 - 0.12 = 0.18; x1.55 = 0.279; x0.90 m = 0.2511; x0.35 = 0.087885 m, rounds to 0.0879. Deliberately sampled away from the first case so the two do not share a root depth or depletion fraction.

b-application-rate._note: 12 lps over 0.8 ha = 15 lps/ha, and that is the unit the printed Q/A ratio actually returns. As a depth rate it would be 15 x 0.36 = 5.4 mm/hr, since 1 lps/ha is 3.6 m3/hr over 10,000 m2 = 0.36 mm/hr. The golden asserts 15, NOT 5.4: folding the 0.36 into the answer would contradict the printed formula. Same situation as the Rational Method entry, where the constant is carried by the units.
4.5 lps over 1.25 ha = 3.6 lps/ha. The second case uses a lower flow and a larger area, so the rate falls well below the first.

b-water-requirement._note: ET + P = 5.4 + 18.2 = 23.6 mm. Both terms are demands on the supply: water leaving through the leaves and surface, and water leaving through the bottom of the root zone. Percolation is added, never subtracted.
8.1 + 6.5 = 14.6 mm. Transpiration-dominated case, the mirror of the first where percolation dominates.

b-evapotranspiration._note: E + T = 4.2 + 6.8 = 11.0 mm/day. Transpiration exceeds evaporation here, so the canopy is closed.
6.5 + 3.1 = 9.6 mm/day. Evaporation exceeds transpiration, the early-season or sparse-canopy case. The total is close to the first case while the split is inverted, which is the point of the pair.

b-water-applied._note: Q = 2.78 (A D)/T with D in MILLIMETRES, which is the basis the printed 2.78 belongs to. 0.75 ha x 60 mm = 45 ha-mm. One ha-mm is 10 m3 = 10000 L, so 45 ha-mm = 450000 L; over 4 h = 14400 s that is exactly 31.25 L/s. The printed constant is the rounded form of 10000/3600 = 2.7778, so the formula returns 31.275 instead of 31.25. The golden asserts the FORMULA output, and the note records the exact figure so the 0.025 gap is never mistaken for a bug. If D were taken in cm the correct constant is 27.78 and 2.78 would give 3.1275, ten times low, which is the first distractor.

2.78 x (1.10 x 35)/6.5 = 2.78 x 38.5/6.5 = 107.03/6.5. Exact physics check: 1.10 ha x 35 mm = 38.5 ha-mm = 385000 L; over 6.5 h = 23400 s that is 16.4529914530 L/s, against 16.4661538462 from the rounded constant. Tolerance stated because the printed 2.78 is not exact.

b-gumbel-return-period._note: Record 52 years, event ranked 2nd. N/(N-m+1) = 52/51 = 1.0196078431; ln = 0.0194180859; ln of that = -3.9415503865. Bracket 0.5772 - 3.9415503865 = -3.3643503865, times -sqrt(6)/pi = -0.7796968, gives K = +2.6231732346. The two nested logs cancelling is the whole point: a short inner log is what makes K large, which is why a 2nd-ranked event on a 52-year record carries a bigger departure than a 10th-ranked one. X_T = 380 + 2.6231732346 x 140 = 747.2442528 mm, rounding to 747. Rank 1 is excluded from the spec because it drives the inner log to zero and K to infinity.

Short record, deep rank: N/(N-m+1) = 30/21 = 1.4285714286; ln = 0.3566749439; ln of that = -1.0309304332. Bracket 0.5772 - 1.0309304332 = -0.4537304332, times -0.7796968 gives K = +0.3537721674, the low end of the spec range. X_T = 520 + 0.3537721674 x 95 = 553.6083559 mm, rounding to 554. A 30-year record cannot resolve a 100-year event, which is exactly why the factor collapses toward 0.35 here. Tolerance stated because the value passes through two nested logarithms and the exact hand arithmetic is only good to about six figures.

b-drop-spillway-capacity._note: C L h^1.5 = 1.7 x 6 x 0.45^1.5. sqrt(0.45) = 0.6708204, so 0.45^1.5 = 0.3018692. 1.7 x 6 = 10.2, times 0.3018692 = 3.0790658 m3/s. Cross-check on the exponent: doubling the head here to 0.90 m gives 1.7 x 6 x 0.853815 = 8.7093, a factor of 2.828, which is 2^1.5 and confirms the three-halves power rather than a linear or quadratic one.

1.55 x 2.5 x 0.8^1.5. 0.8^1.5 = 0.8 x 0.8944272 = 0.7155418. 1.55 x 2.5 = 3.875, times 0.7155418 = 2.7727244 m3/s. The head here is near the top of the spec range, where the h^2 distractor is 0.894x rather than far away, which is the case the cap at h = 0.9 exists to keep clear of the 1% band.

b-dam-top-width._note: 0.55 sqrt(12) + 1. sqrt(12) = 3.4641016, x 0.55 = 1.9052559, + 1 = 2.9052559 m. Order-of-magnitude check: a 12 m embankment gets a 2.9 m crest, not 7.6 m as a linear rule would give.

0.55 sqrt(3.5) + 1. sqrt(3.5) = 1.8708287, x 0.55 = 1.0289558, + 1 = 2.0289558 m. The low-height case, where the additive metre is a third of the answer and dropping it is badly wrong. This is the case that justifies keeping the +1 term in the spec at all.

b-wave-height._note: 0.014 sqrt(20). sqrt(20) = 4.4721360, x 0.014 = 0.0626099 m, i.e. 6.26 cm of crest allowance for a 20 km fetch. Sanity: the same fetch in metres with the same 0.014 gives 0.00198 m, which is 31.6 times smaller and is the unit error the spec is built around. sqrt(1000) = 31.6228 confirms the ratio exactly.

0.014 sqrt(6.5). sqrt(6.5) = 2.5495098, x 0.014 = 0.0356931 m, i.e. 3.57 cm. A short fetch gives a small allowance, as the square root requires: 6.5 km is a third of 20 km but only 0.57 of the allowance, since 6.5/20 = 0.325 and sqrt(0.325) = 0.570.

b-orifice-velocity._note: sqrt(2 x 9.81 x 0.85) = sqrt(16.677) = 4.0837482782 m/s. Check against ft/s: 4.0837482782 x 3.28084 = 13.398125 ft/s, a credible jet velocity for a sluice gate. Doubling the head to 1.70 m gives sqrt(33.354) = 5.7752981, a factor of exactly sqrt(2) = 1.41421, which is the square root and not the doubling a linear rule would predict. An earlier hand value of 4.0837468 was wrong in the sixth decimal; the gate caught it, and the full-precision figure above is the one asserted.

sqrt(2 x 9.81 x 0.12) = sqrt(2.3544) = 1.5344054223 m/s. The low-head case, where the same 0.5 m3/s pipe would be running at a trickle. As a cross-check on the square-root dependence, h = 0.12 is 0.12/0.85 = 0.1411765 of the first case, and the velocity should be sqrt(0.1411765) = 0.3757358 of it: 4.0837482782 x 0.3757358 = 1.5344054, which matches. An earlier hand value of 1.5344063 was wrong in the seventh decimal and the gate caught it.

b-orifice-discharge._note: 0.6 x 0.005 x sqrt(2 x 9.81 x 0.30) = 0.003 x sqrt(5.886) = 0.003 x 2.4261079943 = 0.0072783240 m3/s, i.e. 7.278 lps. The unit check from the SOURCE NOTE: the same orifice as 50 cm2 under 30 cm of head, fed into the PRINTED variable list units with the printed 0.6, gives 0.6 x 50 x sqrt(2 x 9.81 x 30) = 30 x 24.2610799 = 727.8324, exactly 100x this figure. The 100 is 1e4 for cm2 against m2, times 1e-2 for cm against m, times 1e3 for lps against m3/s. Keeping the printed sqrt(2 g h) form but working in the printed cm and lps units, the coefficient that gives the right answer is 0.006: 0.006 x 50 x 24.2610799 = 7.2783 lps, matching. The drill asserts the SI result, which uses the printed 0.6 unchanged.

0.6 x 0.02 x sqrt(2 x 9.81 x 0.75) = 0.012 x sqrt(14.715) = 0.012 x 3.8360135558 = 0.0460321627 m3/s, i.e. 46.03 lps. The area is 4x the first case and the head is 2.5x, so the discharge should rise by 4 x sqrt(2.5) = 4 x 1.5811388 = 6.3245553; measured, 0.0460321627 / 0.0072783240 = 6.3246, which confirms the square-root dependence on head rather than a linear one. An earlier hand value of 0.0460247 came from a mis-squared square root and was rejected by the gate.

b-weir-rectangular-no-contraction._note: Q = 1.84 x 0.45 x 0.36^1.5. sqrt(0.36) = 0.6, so 0.36^1.5 = 0.216. 1.84 x 0.45 = 0.828, times 0.216 = 0.178848 m3/s. Exponent check: doubling the head to 0.72 m gives 1.84 x 0.45 x 0.6109402589 = 0.5058585344, a factor of 2.828427, which is 2^1.5 = 2.828427 rather than the 2 a linear rule would give. Applicability check: L = 0.45 m is under 2.7H = 0.972 m, so the no-contraction form is the correct one here.

1.84 x 0.2 x 0.55^1.5. sqrt(0.55) = 0.7416198487, 0.55^1.5 = 0.4078909168. 1.84 x 0.2 = 0.368, times 0.4078909168 = 0.1501038574 m3/s. The narrow-crest end of the spec: L = 0.2 m against 2.7H = 1.485 m, so the contraction condition is satisfied with room to spare, which is what makes the plain form valid.

b-weir-rectangular-contraction._note: Effective length L - 0.2H = 0.95 - 0.2 x 0.27 = 0.95 - 0.054 = 0.896 m. sqrt(0.27) = 0.5196152423, 0.27^1.5 = 0.1402961154. 1.84 x 0.896 = 1.64864, times 0.1402961154 = 0.2312977877 m3/s. The 0.2H term: omitting it would give 1.84 x 0.95 x 0.1402961154 = 0.2452376097, a factor of 1.060268 on the answer. That gap is the whole reason the head range here is narrow - at 0.2H/L = 0.056842 the omission is worth about 5.684 per cent, comfortably distinguishable, whereas a much smaller head would make it round onto the correct option. Applicability: L = 0.95 m exceeds 2.7H = 0.729 m, so the contracted form applies.

1 - 0.2 x 0.25 = 0.95 m effective length; 0.25^1.5 = 0.125; 1.84 x 0.95 x 0.125 = 0.2185 m3/s. Worst corner of the spec for the omitted-deduction distractor: 0.2H/L = 0.05 exactly, so forgetting the deduction inflates the answer by a factor of 1.052632, the smallest separation anywhere in the spec and still clear of the 1% band.

b-weir-trapezoidal-cipolletti._note: Q = 1.86 x 1.8 x 0.22^1.5. sqrt(0.22) = 0.469041576, 0.22^1.5 = 0.1031891467. 1.86 x 1.8 = 3.348, times 0.1031891467 = 0.3454772632 m3/s. Same arithmetic as the rectangular forms with the Cipolletti constant: at identical inputs the Cipolletti discharge is 1.86/1.84 = 1.01087 of the rectangular one, since the 4H:1L side slope trades a narrowed section against the cancellation of end contractions.

1.86 x 0.75 x 0.3325537551 = 0.4639124883 m3/s, where 0.48^1.5 = 0.3325537551. The larger-head case; against the first Cipolletti case the length ratio is 0.416667 and the head ratio is 2.181818, and the predicted discharge ratio 1.86 x 0.416667 x 3.222759 = 1.342816 matches the measured 0.463912 / 0.345477, confirming the three-halves power.

b-weir-triangular-vnotch._note: Q = 1.4 x 0.3^2.5 = 1.4 x 0.3^2 x sqrt(0.3) = 1.4 x 0.09 x 0.5477225575 = 0.0690130422 m3/s, that is 69.013 lps. This is the exact case quoted in the SOURCE NOTE: with H in metres the printed form reproduces the physical flow, whereas the printed variable list says cm and the same expression on H = 30 gives 6901.3, a hundred times too large. Exponent decomposition check: the area term H^2 = 0.09 and the velocity term sqrt(H) = 0.5477225575, and the flow is strictly their product, which is why a squared-head answer would miss the velocity entirely.

1.4 x 0.08^2.5 = 1.4 x 0.00181019336 = 0.002534270704 m3/s, that is 2.5343 lps. The low-head end, and the reason the spec rounds to 6 decimal places: at 8 cm the flow is under a litre per second while at 30 cm it is 69.01 lps, so the two cases differ by a factor of 27.23 while the heads differ by only 3.75 - the sensitivity of the notch in a nutshell.

b-parshall-flume._note: W = 0.3048 m is the standard 1 ft Parshall throat. W^0.026 = 0.3048^0.026 = 0.9695816532, so the exponent is 1.522 x 0.9695816532 = 1.4757032762, not a constant. Ha^E = 0.15^1.4757 = 0.0608352324. Q = 0.3048 x 0.0608352324 = 0.0185425788 m3/s, that is 18.54 lps. Read this against the SOURCE NOTE rather than as a real flume rating: the same inputs in centimetres send the printed expression to about 2756, and a genuine 1 ft Parshall at 15 cm passes on the order of 45 lps, so neither the centimetre reading nor this metre reading should be presented to a student as a calibrated discharge. The drill exercises the printed algebra.

The standard 5 ft throat. W^0.026 = 1.0110150234, exponent = 1.5387648656; Ha^E = 0.2256242432; Q = 1.524 x 0.2256242432 = 0.3438513466 m3/s, that is 343.9 lps. The width-dependent exponent is visible directly: against the 1 ft case the exponent rises from 1.475703 to 1.538765, and since 0.026 is such a small power on the width a five-fold increase in throat width moves the exponent by only 0.063062. That insensitivity is precisely why a flume rating cannot be scaled from one size to another.

b-submerged-orifice._note: 2 g dh = 2 x 9.81 x 0.18 = 3.5316, sqrt = 1.8792551716 m/s. Q = 0.6 x 0.0125 x 1.8792551716 = 0.0075 x 1.8792551716 = 0.014094413787 m3/s, that is 14.094 lps. The submerged point, which is the whole difference from b-orifice-discharge: the driving head is the 0.18 m DIFFERENCE between the two levels. Had the same pipe been discharging freely under its full upstream head the flow would be larger, and the error of using the upstream level instead of the difference scales with the square root of the ratio of the two heads.

2 x 9.81 x 0.42 = 8.2404, sqrt = 2.8706096913; 0.6 x 0.045 = 0.027; Q = 0.077506461666 m3/s, that is 77.51 lps. Top corner of the spec. Cross-check on the square root: the area is 3.6x the first case and the head difference is 2.3333x, so the discharge should be 3.6 x sqrt(2.3333) = 5.499091; measured, 0.077506 / 0.014094 = 5.499091.

b-partly-filled-orifice._note: sqrt(2 x 9.81 x 0.35) = sqrt(6.867) = 2.6204961362 m/s. Q = 0.62 x 0.024 x 2.6204961362 = 0.01488 x 2.6204961362 = 0.038992982507 m3/s, that is 38.99 lps. The coefficient is a sampled variable here rather than a fixed 0.6, which is the difference from b-orifice-discharge and b-submerged-orifice: at 0.62 this is a sharp-edged entry, and a re-entrant or bellmouth entry would carry closer to 0.8 and pass correspondingly more. Omitting C would give 0.06289190727, a factor of 1.612903.

sqrt(2 x 9.81 x 0.85) = sqrt(16.677) = 4.0837482782; Q = 0.65 x 0.2858623795 = 0.18581054666 m3/s, that is 185.8 lps. Top corner. The three factors are deliberately spread across their ranges: C = 0.65 is the high end of the sharp-edged band, so the omitted-coefficient distractor is only 1.538462x here against 1.666667x at the low end, which is the tightest that option ever gets and still clear.

c-series-circuit._note: 1/10 = 0.1, 1/25 = 0.04, 1/50 = 0.02. The sum of the reciprocals is exactly 0.16 per microfarad inverse, so C_S = 1/0.16 = 6.25 uF. Note the result is smaller than the smallest member, 10 uF, which is the check that distinguishes the inverse sum from the direct sum that would have returned 85 uF. Ordering does not matter here: permuting 10, 25 and 50 leaves the same 0.16.

1/4 = 0.25, 1/8 = 0.125, 1/8 = 0.125. Sum = 0.5, so C_S = 1/0.5 = 2 uF exactly. A case where two members are equal, so it is a cross-check on the arithmetic: two equal 8 uF in series give 4 uF on their own, and putting 4 uF in series with that gives 1/(1/4+1/4) = 2 uF, agreeing.

c-parallel-circuit._note: Bring to a common denominator of 48: 1/12 = 4/48, 1/24 = 2/48, 1/48 = 1/48, so the sum is 7/48 per ohm inverse and R_P = 48/7 = 6.857142857142857 ohm. Geometric check: the doubling ladder 12, 24, 48 should halve at each stage of adding one more doubling branch, and 12/2 = 6, 6/2 = 3, 3/2 = 1.5 would be the case for 6, 12, 24; the 48 case lands at 6.857, just above the 6 of the 12, 24 pair as it should be, since adding a third equal-halving branch always pushes the result up.

1/5 = 0.2, 1/20 = 0.05, 1/80 = 0.0125. Sum = 0.2625, so R_P = 1/0.2625 = 3.809523809523809 ohm. Exact fraction: 0.2625 = 21/80, so R_P = 80/21. The result sits below the smallest branch, 5 ohm, as an inverse sum must. Physical read: with 5 ohm drawing 0.2 A on its own and the other two adding 0.0625 A between them, the 1.7 A total across roughly 1.7 ohm of source resistance is consistent with 3.81 ohm.

c-voltage-divider._note: Ratio 30/100 = 0.3, so V_n = 0.3 x 120 = 36 V. The section asked about carries 30 of the 100 ohm, so it takes 30 percent of the volt and the remaining 70 ohm takes the other 84 V, which sums back to the 120 V supply. Holding the ratio and scaling the supply is the check that the divider is linear in voltage.

Ratio 15/60 = 0.25, so V_n = 0.25 x 240 = 60 V. This is the lower corner of the ratio box at 0.25, and it is a quarter of the supply, so the other 45 ohm carries 180 V. The inverted ratio would have returned 240 x 60/15 = 960 V, which is four times the supply and the clearest signal that the ratio has been turned the wrong way round.

c-current-divider._note: R_total/R_n = 30/100 = 0.3, so I_n = 0.3 x 12 = 3.6 A. The consistency check is that the branch current is well under the 12 A line current, which it must be, and that the remaining 8.4 A is what the other branch carries. Is 30 ohm a real parallel equivalent for a 100 ohm branch? The other branch would be R = 30 x 100/(100 - 30) = 42.857 ohm, a perfectly ordinary value, so the input set is physically consistent.

R_total/R_n = 15/150 = 0.1, so I_n = 0.1 x 20 = 2.0 A, the bottom corner of the ratio box. The other branch then carries 18 A. Consistency: for a 15 ohm parallel equivalent with one branch at 150 ohm the other is 15 x 150/135 = 16.667 ohm, so this is a case where the two branches are within a factor of nine and the currents split 2 to 18, which matches current sharing inversely with resistance.

c-delta-wye._note: R_b x R_c = 20 x 30 = 600, and the sum R_a + R_b + R_c = 10 + 20 + 30 = 60, so R_1 = 600/60 = 10 ohm exactly. The pattern is that the numerator is the product of the two resistors meeting at the node away from R_a, and the denominator is the sum of all three. A familiar case: the 10, 20, 30 delta is close to the 10 ohm per arm wye it converts to, and when all three are equal the conversion gives R/3 on each arm.

R_b x R_c = 100 x 5 = 500, and the sum = 5 + 100 + 5 = 110, so R_1 = 500/110 = 50/11 = 4.545454545454546 ohm. This is the case that shows the conversion is not symmetric in the three arms: R_1 is small because R_a and R_b are large, while an arm built on the two small resistors would be much larger. Every wye arm is less than the smallest delta resistance, which is the check that the conversion has been done the right way round.

c-conductance._note: C = 1/R = 1/0.5 = 2 S exactly. The reciprocal is the whole content of the formula. Dimensional check: an ohm inverted is a siemens, and the two quantities multiply back to unity, so 0.5 ohm x 2 S = 1. Halving the resistance from 1 ohm to 0.5 ohm doubles the conductance from 1 S to 2 S, which is the direction the reciprocal relationship always runs.

C = 1/2.5 = 0.4 S exactly. Reciprocal check: 2.5 x 0.4 = 1. This is the resistance returned unchanged as a distractor, so the two options differ by a factor of 6.25 there and only by the factor 2.5/0.4 = 6.25 here, which is exactly the ratio of R to C and the reason the distractor lands in band over this resistance range.

c-current._note: I = V/Z = 220/55 = 4 A exactly. Both numbers are 220 V, the standard single-phase supply in the Philippines, and a 55 ohm impedance, and the division comes out clean at 4 A. If the winding had been treated as a plain DC resistance of 55 ohm the same current would follow, which is only because this case is purely resistive; the impedance matters whenever there is reactance present.

I = V/Z = 120/40 = 3 A exactly. The inverted form Z/V would have returned 40/120 = 0.333, which is 1/I, so the distractor sits 9x below the answer and lands inside the 100x band. Note that the answer is a per-phase style value for a single-phase winding and that the impedance here is the magnitude, not the resistance component alone.

c-resistance-in-wire._note: R = rho x L / A = 0.0172 x 100 / 25. The numerator is 1.72, and 1.72/25 = 0.0688 ohm. Copper resistivity of 0.0172 ohm-mm2/m is the standard 17.2 nanohm-metre value, and at 100 m of 25 mm2 the result is a fraction of an ohm, which is why a feeder this size needs no more than a tenth of a volt drop over its run at moderate current.

R = 0.0282 x 400 / 10. Numerator = 11.28, and 11.28/10 = 1.128 ohm, the top corner of the box. Aluminium at 0.0282 is 1.64 times the resistivity of copper, and this case also uses the largest length against the smallest area, so the two exaggerating factors compound to 10.0 x 1.64 = 16.4 times the first case, and 0.0688 x 16.4 = 1.128 as expected.

c-composite-wire-resistance._note: ln(20/3) = ln(6.6666667) = 1.897119984886. The prefactor is 0.0172/(2 pi x 50) = 0.0172/314.1592654 = 5.4744004e-5. R = 5.4744004e-5 x 1.897119984886 = 1.0385748e-4 ohm. The sign is the point: the inner radius 3 mm and the outer 20 mm are entered so that r2/r1 is greater than 1 and the logarithm is positive, since the handbook prints the labels the other way round. A result of about 0.104 milliohm is the right order for a short electrode in good soil.

ln(40/2) = ln(20) = 2.995732273554. The prefactor is 0.029/(2 pi x 200) = 0.029/1256.6370614 = 2.30740e-5. R = 2.30740e-5 x 2.995732273554 = 6.91198e-5 ohm. Cross-check on the two mechanisms that drive the result: the prefactor here is 0.4213 of the first case (length up 4x, resistivity up 1.686x), and the logarithm is 1.579x larger (radius ratio 20 against 6.667), so the answer should be 0.4213 x 1.579 = 0.6653 of the first, and 6.91198e-5 / 1.0385748e-4 = 0.6656, agreeing to four figures.

c-frequency._note: f = P x N / 120 = 4 x 1800 / 120 = 7200/120 = 60 Hz exactly. This is the canonical case: a four-pole machine on the 60 Hz supply standard in the Philippines has a synchronous speed of 1800 rpm, and the nameplate running speed of about 1750 rpm sits just under it, the difference being slip.

f = 6 x 900 / 120 = 5400/120 = 45 Hz exactly. A six-pole machine turning at 900 rpm. Cross-check: the synchronous speed of a six-pole machine on 60 Hz would be 120 x 60/6 = 1200 rpm, so 900 rpm is 75 percent of that and this case corresponds to 45 Hz rather than 60, which is the consistency the formula exists to establish.

c-percent-slip._note: The shortfall is 1800 - 1740 = 60 rpm, and 60/1800 = 0.0333333, so slip = 3.333333 percent. This is the ordinary running figure for a healthy induction motor, where 3 to 5 percent is normal at full load. The rotor never reaches the field speed, and this is the whole mechanism: at exactly 1800 rpm there would be no relative motion, no induced current and no torque at all.

The shortfall is 1780 - 1700 = 80 rpm, and 80/1780 = 0.0449438, so slip = 4.49438202247191 percent. Note the field speed here is 1780 rather than a textbook 1800, which is a machine running a little under its nominal frequency, and slip is measured against the actual field speed rather than the nominal one.

c-percent-regulation._note: The drop is 240 - 200 = 40 V, and 40/200 = 0.2, so regulation = 20 percent exactly, the top corner of the box. This is a high figure and it is what a source with appreciable internal impedance produces under heavy load, and it is why a long rural feeder is sized on voltage drop rather than on loss.

The drop is 225 - 215 = 10 V, and 10/215 = 0.0465116, so regulation = 4.651162790697674 percent, the bottom corner. A tight source: under 5 percent droop from no load to full load. The denominator being the full-load voltage rather than the no-load voltage is what keeps this at 4.65 rather than the 4.44 that the no-load denominator would have given.

c-horsepower._note: Numerator 2 pi x 50 x 1200 = 2 x 3.14159265359 x 50 x 1200 = 376991.118430775. Dividing by 44760 = 60 x 746 gives 8.42236774736 hp. The divisor is the whole content of this case: the same numerator divided by 33,000 instead, the constant that belongs to torque in kilogram-force metres, would give 11.4234, about 36 percent high, and the printed form with no divisor at all would give 376991.

Numerator 2 pi x 200 x 1800 = 2261946.71029265, and 2261946.71029265 / 44760 = 50.534639 hp. Cross-check against the first case: torque is 4x and speed is 1.5x, so the power should be 6x, and 8.4223677 x 6 = 50.5342, agreeing to four figures. The relationship is exactly linear in both torque and speed, which is the check that the divisor is right.

c-motor-hp-from-engine._note: hp = 45 x 2/3 = 30 hp exactly. The two-thirds is a derating, and 30 out of 45 is the size of motor a workshop would actually put on a 45 hp engine block so that the engine can ride through the starting transient. The arithmetic is trivial; the reasoning behind the factor is the part worth remembering.

hp = 10 x 2/3 = 6.666666666666667 hp. Small engine, small motor. The exact value is 20/3, and it is a case where the nameplate would in practice be rounded to a standard 7.5 hp frame, which is the reason these figures are treated as sizing guides rather than as catalogue entries.

c-locked-rotor-current._note: LRC = VA/V = 10000/220 = 45.45454545454545 A. The horsepower cancels in the printed product, so the motor rating does not enter at all. For a 220 V machine 10 kVA of apparent power implies a locked rotor draw near 45 A, which is several times a running current of 12 to 15 A, and it is that figure the protective device has to be set for.

LRC = 6000/440 = 13.636363636363637 A. The 440 V case draws exactly half the current of the 220 V case for twice the kVA per amp, which is the point of the doubled voltage on a three-phase distribution feeder. Compare with dividing by the square root of three times the voltage, the line-to-neutral slip, which would have given 7.87 A.

c-capacitive-reactance._note: 2 pi x 60 x 25e-6: 60 x 25e-6 = 1.5e-3, and 2 pi x 1.5e-3 = 9.42477796076938e-3, so X_c = 1/9.42477796076938e-3 = 106.103295394597 ohm. The classic motor starting value: a 25 uF capacitor on 60 Hz presents about 106 ohm. Reciprocal check on the structure: doubling C to 50 uF halves the reactance to 53.05, and halving f to 30 Hz would double it to 212.2.

2 pi x 50 x 100e-6: 50 x 100e-6 = 5e-3, and 2 pi x 5e-3 = 0.0314159265358979, so X_c = 1/0.0314159265358979 = 31.8309886183791 ohm, the bottom corner. The same part as the first case at 50 Hz would present 127.3 ohm, since 60/50 = 1.2, and the capacitance here is 4x, so the reactance should be 1.2/4 = 0.3 of the 106.103 of the first case, and 31.831/106.103 = 0.300, confirming it.

c-inductive-reactance._note: 2 pi x 60 x 0.05 = 2 pi x 3 = 6 pi = 18.8495559215388 ohm. The reciprocal of the capacitive case at the same frequency and capacitance, and note it is the same arithmetic: 2 pi f times the reactance of the component. A 50 mH coil at 60 Hz is about 18.85 ohm.

2 pi x 50 x 1.5 = 2 pi x 75 = 150 pi = 471.238898038469 ohm, the top corner. Cross-check against the first case: 50/60 times 1.5/0.05 gives 0.8333 x 30 = 25, and 18.8495559 x 25 = 471.2389, agreeing exactly. The scaling is linear in both frequency and inductance, which is the whole of the result.

c-rlc-series._note: The net reactance is 100 - 5 = 95 ohm, and 95^2 = 9025. Adding R^2 = 20^2 = 400 gives 9425, and sqrt(9425) = 97.081380453. Vector check: the resistive leg is 400/9425 = 4.2 percent of the total squared, so the impedance is within about 2 percent of the reactive leg, which is what a badly under-compensated tuned circuit looks like. The arithmetic sum would have been 115, some 18 percent high.

The net reactance is 250 - 20 = 230 ohm, squared to 52900. R^2 = 120^2 = 14400, and the total is 67300, whose root is 259.422433. The arithmetic sum would be 350, some 35 percent high, which is the error this formula exists to prevent. Note the in-phase leg is now the larger of the two, 120 against 230 but squared 14400 against 52900, so the answer still sits close to the reactive leg rather than to the sum.

c-rlc-parallel._note: The net reactive current is 20 - 1.5 = 18.5 A, squared to 342.25. I_R^2 = 6^2 = 36, and the total is 378.25, whose root is 19.4486. Clean case: the arithmetic sum of the three branch currents would be 27.5 A, some 41 percent high. Correcting the 3 A capacitive current against the 20 A inductive one has pulled the line current down to just under the inductive branch alone would suggest once the resistive 6 A is added.

The net reactive current is 40 - 3 = 37 A, squared to 1369. I_R^2 = 20^2 = 400, and the total is 1769, whose root is 42.0595. Here the in-phase leg matters more: 400 of 1769 is 23 percent, so the line current is noticeably above the 40 A the inductor alone would draw. The arithmetic sum of 63 A would be 50 percent high, the largest proportional error in this box.

c-rlc-voltage._note: The net reactive voltage is 200 - 10 = 190 V, squared to 36100. V_R^2 = 40^2 = 1600, and the total is 37700, whose root is 194.1649. The arithmetic sum would be 250 V, 28.5 percent high. The interesting point of this case is that the inductor alone carries 200 V, which is larger than the 194 V total the source had to supply, and that is normal rather than a contradiction.

The net reactive voltage is 400 - 40 = 360 V, squared to 129600. V_R^2 = 240^2 = 57600, and the total is 187200, whose root is 432.6647. Both legs are now substantial, and the in-phase leg is 31 percent of the total squared, so the answer sits well away from either component. The arithmetic sum of 680 V would be 57 percent high, the widest spread in this spec.

c-transformer-voltage-ratio._note: The turns ratio is 200/400 = 0.5, so V_s = 220 x 0.5 = 110 V exactly. A 400-turn primary with a 200-turn secondary is a 2:1 step-down, and 220 V in gives 110 V out. The inverted ratio would have returned 440 V, a clean double, and the squared ratio 55 V, half the answer, so the two structural errors here are a factor of four apart from each other and neither is close to the result.

The turns ratio is 200/240 = 0.83333, so V_s = 480 x 0.83333 = 400 V exactly. This is the shallowest step-down in the box, 480 V down to 400 V, and it is the corner that keeps the turns ratio strictly below 1. With a 240-turn primary and 200-turn secondary the ratio is 1.2:1, and the arithmetic works out to a round 400 V because 480/1.2 = 400.

c-transformer-power-relation._note: The primary volt-amperes are 220 x 10 = 2200 VA, and 2200/110 = 20 A exactly. The power checks out on both sides: 110 V x 20 A = 2200 VA, the same as the primary product, which is the whole content of the relation. The secondary carries twice the primary current for half the voltage, as a 2:1 step-down must.

The primary volt-amperes are 440 x 12 = 5280 VA, and 5280/70 = 75.4286 A, the top corner. This is an 6.29:1 step-down from 440 V to 70 V, so the secondary current is more than six times the primary, and 70 x 75.4286 = 5280 VA, confirming the power balance. The separation of the voltage boxes is what keeps this a genuine step-down across every sample.

c-transformer-current-turns._note: The turns ratio is 600/200 = 3, so I_s = 10 x 3 = 30 A exactly. A 3:1 step-down turns 10 A at the primary into 30 A at the secondary. Power check across the ratio: the secondary voltage would be a third of the primary, so 3 x 30 against 1 x 10 leaves the product unchanged, which is the reason the current ratio runs opposite to the voltage ratio.

The turns ratio is 300/200 = 1.5, so I_s = 5 x 1.5 = 7.5 A. The shallowest step-down in the box, and the corner that holds the ratio strictly above 1 so the secondary current always exceeds the primary. At a ratio of 1.5 the current is up one half while the voltage is down a third, so the two multiply back to the same power.

c-electrical-unit-conversions._note: D = 100 mils, D^2 = 10000, and pi x 10000 = 31415.9265358979, divided by 4 = 7853.98163397448 sq mil. The cross-check that ties the family together: circular mil is D^2 = 10000, and 10000/7853.98 = 1.2732, which is 4/pi and is exactly the 1.273 the printed note quotes between a circular mil and a square mil. So this drill and the circular-mil identity are two halves of the same relation.

D = 40 mils, D^2 = 1600, pi x 1600 = 5026.54824574367, divided by 4 = 1256.63706143592 sq mil. Cross-check the two cases: the diameter ratio is 100/40 = 2.5, and the area ratio should be the square of that, 6.25, and 7853.98163397448/1256.63706143592 = 6.25 exactly. Area scales with the square of diameter, as it must, and this is why a wire table quotes circular mils as D squared.

c-temperature-conversions._note: 212 degF is the boiling point of water, so the answer must be exactly 100 degC. 212 - 32 = 180, and 180 x 5/9 = 100. This is the single reference point that validates the whole printed identity, and it sits above the drill box only because the box stops at 200 degF to keep the shifted distractor clear of the 1.15 scalar.
98.6 degF is human body temperature. 98.6 - 32 = 66.6, and 66.6 x 5/9 = 37.0 degC, confirming the 37 degC that the identity was built on.

c-stefan-boltzmann._note: A surface at 900 K over 5 m2 at emissivity 0.95. 900^4 = 6.561e11, and 5.669e-8 x 6.561e11 = 37196.4 W per m2 per unit emissivity, so times 5 m2 times 0.95 the answer is 176682 W. The magnitude is the point: radiation from a hot surface is tens of kilowatts from a few square metres.

450 K is exactly half of 900 K, and a fourth power makes that a sixteenth, not a half. Per m2 at emissivity 0.8: 450^4 = 4.1006e10, and 5.669e-8 x 4.1006e10 = 2324.9 W/m2, and 2324.9/37196.4 = 0.0625, which is 1/16 exactly. That is the fourth power doing its work, and it is why the kelvin scale is not optional.

c-first-law-thermodynamics._note: The textbook balance, and the reason for the SOURCE NOTE on this formula. 1000 J of heat enters and 300 J of work leaves, so 700 J is retained. The printed Q + W would give 1300 J, which is energy appearing from nothing; the drill uses the difference because the printed definition of W is work done BY the system.

2400 J of heat in, 600 J of work out, 1800 J retained. Here W/Q = 0.25, and the printed sum would be 3000 J against a true 1800 J - a 1.67x error, which is the size of mistake the printed plus sign invites at ordinary ratios.

c-newtons-law-cooling._note: 25 W/m2K over 2.4 m2 across a 40 K difference. 25 x 2.4 = 60, and 60 x 40 = 2400 W, the 2.4 kW a dairy chiller is rated on. Note the difference is a difference: 65 - 25 = 40, and converting both to kelvin would give the same 40, which is why that error is not offered.

12.5 W/m2K over 8 m2 across a 65 K difference. 12.5 x 8 = 100, and 100 x 65 = 6500 W. The 8 m2 is the total fin surface rather than the plan area of the evaporator, which is the whole reason fins are fitted.

c-fouriers-law._note: Cylindrical wall: 2 pi K L dT over ln(ro/ri). r_o/r_i = 100/40 = 2.5, and ln 2.5 = 0.916291. The numerator is 2 pi x 0.18 x 2 x 60 = 135.717, so 135.717/0.916291 = 148.1 W. For comparison the flat-wall form KA dT/L on the same figures gives 3.4 W, so the log is worth a factor of 43 here.

A thin sleeve: r_o/r_i = 60/50 = 1.2, and ln 1.2 = 0.182322. The numerator is 2 pi x 40 x 1.5 x 130 = 49008.8, so 49008.8/0.182322 = 268805 W. A thin wall is where the log is nearly 1 and the flat-wall answer nearly suffices, which is the limit of the correction.

c-heat-utilization-factor._note: Air enters the heater at 30 degC and leaves it at 80 degC, a 50 K rise available, and the exhaust air at 50 degC has taken 20 K of it. HUF = 20/50 = 0.4. The printed form computes (T3 - T2)/(T1 - T2) = -30/-50, and the two negatives are what make it come out positive.

Full utilisation: the exhaust air leaves at the inlet temperature of 28 degC, so all 42 K of the rise was used. HUF = (45 - 70)/(28 - 70) = -25/-42 = 0.5952. 1.0 is the limit, reached when T_3 equals T_1.

c-humidity-ratio._note: The PRINTED form, W = p_v/P_atm, which is a pressure ratio. 2/101.3 = 0.019744. The psychrometric mass ratio would be 0.622 x 2/(101.3 - 2) = 0.012525, so the printed form is high by a factor of 1.577, which is the gap the SOURCE NOTE records and the reason both mass-ratio forms are offered as distractors.

3.5 kPa of vapour in 98.7 kPa, at the cooler end of the station pressure range. 3.5/98.7 = 0.035461. The mass ratio is 0.622 x 3.5/(98.7 - 3.5) = 0.022846, and the printed form is high by the same 1.552 factor as the first case, as it must be since the factor depends only on the pressure ratio.

c-saturation-ratio._note: 0.012 kg of water per kg of air against a saturation capacity of 0.030, so the air is at 40 percent of saturation. 0.012/0.03 = 0.4 exactly. A value of 1.0 is saturated air, and the 0.028 floor of the W_sat box is what keeps the ratio below that in every sample.

0.006 against 0.028, the tightest corner of the box. 0.006/0.028 = 0.214286. This is the case that set the W_sat floor: the moisture-deficit distractor bottoms out at 0.028 x 0.010/0.018 = 0.0156 of the answer here, and at 0.0035 if the floor were 0.021, which is below the 1 percent plausibility limit.

c-density-specific-volume._note: 300 kg occupying 1.5 m3 is a density of 200 kg/m3, and the specific volume is its reciprocal. 1.5/300 = 0.005 m3/kg exactly, and 1/0.005 = 200 confirms it. Grain, and the kind of bulk that makes a specific volume worth quoting at all.

The tightest corner of the box: 400 kg in 0.2 m3 is a density of 2000 kg/m3, which is steel, and the specific volume is 0.2/400 = 0.0005 m3/kg. This case is the reason the mass and volume ranges are what they are: it is the corner that decides how wide they can be.

c-stress._note: 20 kN over a 200 mm2 pin. Newtons per square millimetre is the megapascal directly, so 20000/200 = 100 MPa, with no conversion in the path. 100 MPa is a sensible working figure for a pin in a farm machine linkage.

125 kN over 2500 mm2, the top corner of both ranges. 125000/2500 = 50 MPa, and the area is 50 mm on a side, so the perimeter error would have given 125000/(4 x 50) = 625, which is 12.5x the answer and the reason that distractor is built from the square root.

c-board-foot._note: 144 in of 6 in wide stock 1.5 in thick. 0.125 ft is 1.5 in, so the volume is 144 x 6 x 1.5 = 1296 cubic inches. One board foot is 1 in x 12 in x 1 ft = 144 cubic inches, and 1296/144 = 9 Bd.Ft. The formula gets there as 144 x 6 x 0.125 / 12 = 9, and the two routes agreeing is the check that the divisor of 12 is the definition rather than a fudge.

96 in of 4 in wide stock a full foot thick is 96 x 4 x 12 = 4608 cubic inches, so 4608/144 = 32 Bd.Ft. The formula gives 96 x 4 x 1 / 12 = 32. A one-foot thickness is at the top of the box and is the timber case rather than the sheet-goods case.

The definition of the unit, and the only case in this batch that checks the divisor head-on. One foot of a 1x12 an inch thick is 12 in x 12 in x 12 in = 1728 cubic inches, and 1728/144 = 12 board feet exactly. The formula gives 12 x 12 x 1 / 12 = 12. This sits below the box floor of 24 in on purpose: it is a definitional check, not a drill sample.

c-board-foot-from-log._note: Doyle on a 16 in small end over a 16 ft log. (16 - 4)^2 = 144, and 144 x 16 / 16 = 144 Bd.Ft. The length dividing out entirely is a useful confirmation that the divisor really is 16 and not 12, since the squared-inch section has to become board feet.

A 20 in small end over 12 ft. (20 - 4)^2 = 256, and 256 x 12 / 16 = 192 Bd.Ft. Doyle understates small logs, which is why 192 Bd.Ft here is an estimate rather than a measurement, and why the rule is used for rough screening and not for settling tonnage.

c-belt-speed._note: V = pi N D in m/min, because rev/min times a circumference in metres is metres per MINUTE. 900 rpm on a 300 mm pulley is 270 pi = 848.23 m/min, which is 14.14 m/s - comfortably inside the 25 to 30 m/s at which centrifugal tension starts to lift a V-belt off the pulley. Using the radius instead would halve it, and dropping the pi gives 270 m/min.

720 rpm on a 250 mm pulley is 180 pi = 565.49 m/min, or 9.42 m/s. A slower drive and a smaller pulley than the case above, and the belt speed falls by a factor of 1.5 rather than by the 2.67 that the speed change alone would suggest, because the diameter moved too.

c-belt-power._note: The belt always carries MORE than the water, and this is the smallest number that shows why. 3.7 kW of fluid power at 55 percent pump efficiency means the shaft is absorbing 3.7/0.55 = 6.727 kW. Multiplying instead of dividing would give 2.035 kW, which is less than the water power and physically impossible.

15 kW delivered to the water at 62 percent, so 15/0.62 = 24.194 kW on the belt. The 61 percent difference between the two figures is exactly the loss the formula is there to expose, and it is the margin by which a drive sized on fluid power is undersized.

The perfect-pump bound, above the box ceiling of 0.7. At E = 1 the belt power equals the fluid power exactly, which is the limit the division is measuring distance from: a real pump sits somewhere below 1 and always needs a larger belt than its water power suggests. This case is worth having because the answer equals the numerator, which makes the direction of the formula obvious in one line.

c-pump-laws._note: The head-square law, N_2 = N_1 (H_2/H_1)^(1/2). Going from 6 m to 60 m of head is a factor of 10, and the square root of 10 is 3.162278, so 1200 rpm becomes 3794.7 rpm. The half power is the entire content: a 10x head needs 3.16x the speed, NOT 10x, and using the first power would ask for 12000 rpm.

1450 rpm with the head rising from 8.5 m to 75 m. The ratio is 75/8.5 = 8.823529, its square root is 2.970108, and 1450 x 2.970108 = 4306.66 rpm. Note the speed more than doubles for less than a tenfold head, which is why trimming a pump up in speed is an efficient way to chase a head that is only a little short.

THE COLLISION POINT, and the reason the two head ranges in this spec are disjoint. With H_1 = H_2 the ratio is 1, and 1 raised to any power is 1, so the first-power option, the third-power option and the 0.85 scalar ALL become exactly N_1 = 1200. Any box that permitted equal heads would render the same option three times. The drill floors H_1 at 12 m and floors H_2 at 50 m, so the ratio is never below 4.167 and never 1. This case is outside the box by construction and is kept as the record.

c-fan-laws._note: The printed fan relation regrouped, with head at the quarter power and flow at the half power. From 450 mm at 35 mm and 3.5 cfm up to 60 mm and 60 cfm: (35/60)^(1/4) = 0.873917 for the head factor and (60/3.5)^(1/2) = 4.140510 for the flow factor, and 450 x 0.873917 x 4.140510 = 1628.3 mm. A 3.1x flow rise bought only 0.6x on the head, and the quarter power is the reason the impeller has to grow at all.

300 mm at 30 mm of pressure and 2 cfm, up to 50 mm and 40 cfm. (30/50)^(1/4) = 0.880112 and (40/2)^(1/2) = 4.472136, and 300 x 0.880112 x 4.472136 = 1180.8 mm. Notice the head factor is barely below 1 even though the head rose by 67 percent, which is the practical signature of the quarter power and the reason fan impellers are large.

THE COLLISION POINT, twice over, and the reason this spec needed three attempts. With equal heads the head factor is 1, and with equal flows the flow factor is 1, so the answer, the doubled-head-exponent option and the doubled-flow-exponent option are all D_1 = 400. An earlier version of this box also collided at intermediate points, where the two doubling options are equal whenever (Q_2/Q_1)^2 = H_2/H_1. The ranges here are disjoint twice over - heads 30..40 against 48..70, flows 2..5 against 25..90 - so no sampled input can reach either collision.

c-air-power._note: Air power, and the dimensional check in one line. 12.5 m3/s against 2.5 m of air head at a specific weight of 12.00 N/m3 gives 12.5 x 12 x 2.5 = 375 W exactly. The argument for why H is a LENGTH: 1 m3/s through 1 m of air head needs 12 N of force, so 12 W. If H were a pressure in pascals the product would be N^2/(s m^2), which is not a power, and the g is already inside the specific weight.

A warm-afternoon reading: 12.25 N/m3 is the specific weight of air at roughly 25 degC, so this is denser than the 12.00 of the case above and sits inside the 11.0 to 12.5 box. 4.2 m3/s against 1.75 m of head is 4.2 x 12.25 x 1.75 = 90.04 W. Note the specific weight moves by only about 8 percent across the whole plausible temperature range, which is why it is nearly a constant in fan sizing.

c-propeller-fan-pitch._note: Pitch is advance per revolution, so it has to come out as a length. At 30 degrees on a 0.75 m radius: 2 pi x 0.75 = 4.712389 m of circumference per revolution, and tan 30 deg = 0.577350, so the advance is 4.712389 x 0.577350 = 2.720699 m. The check is geometric - a 30 degree blade angle should advance a third of the circumference, and 2.720699/4.712389 is 0.5774, which is tan 30.

A finer pitch on a larger fan. 2 pi x 1.2 = 7.539822 m of circumference, and tan 20 deg = 0.363970, so 7.539822 x 0.363970 = 2.744106 m. The pitch is almost unchanged from the 30 degree case despite a 60 percent larger radius, which is the practical reason blade angle and fan diameter are specified independently.

c-specific-speed-dryer-fan._note: Specific speed in the printed units of rpm, cfm and inches of water. 1200 rpm at 3000 cfm and 2.00 in-H2O: sqrt(3000) = 54.772256 and 2^0.75 = 1.681793, so 1200 x 54.772256 / 1.681793 = 39081.7. A five-figure index, and the reason the answer is meaningless as a bare number - the same fan in SI would report a completely different specific speed.

900 rpm at 1200 cfm and 1.50 in-H2O. sqrt(1200) = 34.641016 and 1.5^0.75 = 1.355403, so 900 x 34.641016 / 1.355403 = 23002.6. Halving the flow and dropping the pressure by a quarter has cut the index by 41 percent, which is how sharply specific speed responds to both variables at once.

THE COLLISION POINT, and the reason the pressure box floors at 1.2 rather than 0.5. The two pressure misreadings sit at P_s^(+1/4) and P_s^(-1/4) of the answer, and at P_s = 1 both of those are exactly 1, so the two options render as the same string. Nothing about the ratios reveals this - it only shows up when you ask what they are EQUAL to. The drill box runs 1.2 to 3, so 1 is unreachable, and this case stands outside it as the record.

c-moisture-weight-balance._note: 1200 kg as received less 350 kg oven-dry gives 850 kg of water; the balance checks, 850 + 350 = 1200.
1010 kg as received less 400 kg oven-dry gives 610 kg of water; 610 + 400 = 1010.
Reference point: with no water in the grain the difference is zero and the balance degenerates to W_i = W_o.

c-wet-dry-basis-relationship._note: 14 percent wet basis means the dry matter is 86 percent of the mass, so water per unit dry matter is 14/86; 14 x 100/86 = 16.279069 percent on a dry basis.
22 percent wet: 2200/78 = 28.205128 percent dry, which is 28 percent larger than the wet-basis figure - the gap widens as the grain dries.
Reference point: at zero moisture the two bases coincide, since 0 x 100/100 = 0. It is the only point at which they are equal.

c-weight-moisture-removed._note: 2000 kg at 0.24 to 0.08: the dry matter is 2000 x 0.92 = 1840 kg, which at 8 percent is 1840/0.92 = 2000 kg of final grain, so nothing was removed. Degenerate case, and the printed form agrees: 2000 x 0.16/0.92 = 0.
5000 kg from 0.35 to 0.10: dry matter 3250 kg, final grain 3250/0.90 = 3611.111 kg, so 1388.889 kg of water left. Printed form: 5000 x 0.25/0.90.

c-final-weight-dried._note: 5000 kg from 0.35 to 0.10 gives 3611.111 kg dried, computed from the dry matter side: 5000 x 0.65/0.90. The same figure the moisture-removed case reaches from the other direction.
1000 kg from 0.20 to 0.05: dry matter 800 kg, and 800/0.95 = 842.105 kg dried. 842.105 + 157.895 = 1000, so the mass balance closes.

c-moisture-reduction-rate._note: 10000 kg down to 2000 kg over 8 h removes 8000 kg, so 1000 kg/h.
6000 kg down to 1500 kg over 4.5 h removes 4500 kg, so 1000 kg/h again - a check that the answer is a rate rather than a batch total.
Reference point: no water removed means a zero rate however long the run takes.

c-percent-moisture-reduction._note: 20 percent to 12 percent over 5 h is 8/5 = 1.6 percent per hour. The standard percent reduction would be 100 x 8/20 = 40 percent with no time term, which is the naming clash the SOURCE NOTE records.
26 percent to 10 percent over 8 h is 16/8 = 2 percent per hour.

c-paddy-porosity-medium._note: 69.05 - 0.885 x 25 = 69.05 - 22.125 = 46.925 percent. The long-grain line at the same moisture gives 53.675, and the 6.75 point gap is the class difference.
Reference point: at zero moisture the slope term vanishes and the porosity is the intercept, 69.05 percent.

c-paddy-porosity-long._note: 65.55 - 0.475 x 25 = 65.55 - 11.875 = 53.675 percent, the same figure cross-checked against the medium-grain line above.
Reference point: the long-grain intercept is 65.55, BELOW the medium-grain intercept of 69.05 - the fact the medium-grain coefficient-swap distractor contradicts at the dry end.

c-percent-increase-porosity._note: Porosity 50 to 60 is 10/60 x 100 = 16.666667 percent. The printed denominator is the final porosity; dividing by the initial would give 20 percent.
Porosity 52 to 55 is 3/55 x 100 = 5.454545 percent, against 5.769231 for the initial-value convention.

c-minimum-angle-friction._note: atan(0.5) = 0.4636476 rad = 26.565051 degrees, the 3-4-5 triangle angle.
atan(0.25) = 0.2449787 rad = 14.036243 degrees. The reciprocal atan(4) is 75.963757 degrees and the two sum to exactly 90, which is the identity behind that distractor band.
Reference point: at x = 1 the answer is 45 degrees and the reciprocal distractor atan(1/1) is also 45, so the two coincide. The box stops at 0.7.

c-specific-heat-paddy._note: 0.22008 + 0.01301 x 14 = 0.22008 + 0.18214 = 0.40222 BTU/lb F. The slope implies 1.301 for the water term against 1.0 tabulated.
0.22008 + 0.01301 x 26 = 0.22008 + 0.33826 = 0.55834 BTU/lb F, just over double the dry-matter term.
Reference point: zero moisture leaves the intercept, 0.22008 BTU/lb F, the specific heat of the dry matter.

c-hulling-coefficient._note: 1700 kg of brown rice off 2000 kg of paddy is 0.85, the textbook huller figure. The identical weight pair appears at 85.0 in the brown-rice-recovery goldens, because the two specs are one measurement.
The box corner: 1632/2040 = 0.8 exactly, the lightest allowed brown rice against the heaviest paddy.
The top corner: 1800/2000 = 0.9, the wrong side of the working band.
Reference point: with no husk the coefficient is 1.0, and the inverted distractor W_P/W_BR is also 1.0, so the two options print the same string.

c-wholeness-coefficient._note: 779 kg of whole brown rice out of 820 kg is 0.95, the wholeness a well-set huller holds.
760/900 = 0.844444, the bottom of the box, where the broken share is 15.6 percent.
Reference point: W_WBR = W_BR means no breakage, wholeness 1.0, and the inverted distractor coincides with the answer. The box keeps the ranges disjoint so no sample lands here.

c-hulling-efficiency._note: 1700 kg of WHOLE brown rice off 2000 kg of paddy is 0.85, the product of the two previous coefficients at once.
The bottom corner, 1632/2040 = 0.8, the same weight pair as the hulling spec corner; E_H equals C_H here because the brown rice happens to be whole.
Reference point: a huller that loses nothing gives efficiency 1.0, where the inverted option also prints 1.

c-throughput-capacity._note: 0.2 x 1000 kg over 2 h is also 100 kg/h - the rate does not depend on the batch once the time scales with it.
The box ceiling: 0.2 x 10000 kg over 2 h is 1000 kg/h, the widest span in the batch.
0.2 x 10000 kg over 24 h is 83.333... kg/h, the slow-shift average.

c-brown-rice-per-hour._note: 1000 x 0.75 x 0.96 = 720 kg/h, which is 72 percent of the batch - three haircuts, not one.
5000 x 0.85 x 0.99 = 4207.5 kg/h, the box corner: even the best factors only yield four fifths of the batch.
1000 x 0.65 x 0.93 = 604.5 kg/h, the worst corner. The factors multiply rather than average, which is why the span between corners is so wide.

c-purity._note: [1 - 20/2000] x 100 = [1 - 0.01] x 100 = 99 percent. Twenty grams of removal on two kilos.
[1 - 270/1800] x 100 = 85 percent. The removal is measured on the CLEANED weight, so 270 g out of 2070 (13 percent of the input) reads as 15 percent.
Reference point: W_u = W_c means nothing was removed, purity 100, and the removal distractor drops to zero.

c-percent-brown-rice-recovery._note: (1700/2000) x 100 = 85.0 - the same ratio and the same weight pair as the first hulling-coefficient golden, pinning the two-unit identity between the specs.
(1632/2040) x 100 = 80.0, the bottom corner, the same pair as the hulling spec bottom corner.
Reference point: no husk gives recovery 100, where the inverted distractor also prints 100.0.

c-percent-broken-milled-rice._note: 200/1800 x 100 = 11.111... percent, the bottom corner and the best the box posts.
350/1000 x 100 = 35 percent, the top corner, a machine wrecking its output.
Reference point: half the batch broken gives 50 percent, where the intact-share distractor also returns exactly 50.

c-percent-brewers-rice._note: 80/1000 x 100 = 8 percent, a typical routed product.
50/2000 x 100 = 2.5 percent, the box floor that anchors the distractor band.

c-percent-head-rice-recovery._note: 800/1000 x 100 = 80 percent, the industry reference a buyer grades on.
792/1100 x 100 = 72 percent, the bottom corner: the head rice range starts at 792 to hold the ratio above 0.72.
850/1000 x 100 = 85 percent, the top corner of the tightest box in the batch.
